chapters.name: Chapter 1: Plan the move and translate your skills

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Using the Transition Assistance Program
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the TAP workshops and services that fit your next step.
This lesson builds toward: Given your main path (job, school, trade or business), you will choose the TAP workshops or veterans job services that fit your next step, naming at least two and how to reach them.
The Transition Assistance Program (TAP) helps service members and their spouses get ready for civilian life. It is a joint effort of the Departments of Labor, Defense, Veterans Affairs, Education and Homeland Security, the Small Business Administration and the Office of Personnel Management.
The Department of Labor's part of TAP includes a one-day Employment Fundamentals of Career Transition workshop on job search tools, and a two-day Department of Labor Employment Workshop on resumes, networking, job searching, interviewing and negotiating. There is also an optional two-day Career and Credential Exploration track for choosing a career and planning how to get there.
One-on-one help is offered too: the Employment Navigator and Partnership Program gives career help to transitioning service members and spouses at select installations. Spouses and caregivers have their own workshops. If you cannot attend in person, online learning may count, with approval from your TAP manager or counselor.
Start early. Ask your installation's TAP office when you must begin and which workshops fit your plan: a job, school, a trade, or your own business. Already out? DOL's veterans employment services page lists resources in each state.
Step by step:
- Contact your installation's TAP office and ask when you must start.
- Decide your main path: job, school, trade or business.
- Sign up for the workshops that fit, such as the DOL Employment Workshop.
- Ask about one-on-one help and spouse workshops.
- Already separated? Find your state's veterans resources on dol.gov/agencies/vets.
Words to know:
- TAP: Transition Assistance Program: classes and help for service members moving to civilian life.
- Separation: leaving active military service.
- Credential: a license or certificate that proves a skill.
Official sources:
- DOL VETS: Transition Assistance Program
- DOL VETS: Veterans employment services
Try it now: Write your main path (job, school, trade or business) and the two TAP workshops or services that fit it best. If you are already out, find your state on DOL's veterans employment services page and write down one resource and how to contact it.
You can now choose the TAP workshops and veterans job services that fit your next step.

check.q: Who can take part in DOL's TAP services?
options: Only officers
Transitioning service members and their spouses
Only people who already have a job
Only retirees
check.why: TAP services are for transitioning service members, and spouses can take part too.

check.q: You plan to start a trade after you separate. What do you do first?
options: Skip TAP because it is only for office jobs
Wait until after you separate to think about it
Ask a friend to choose for you
Write your path and pick the TAP workshops or services that fit it
check.why: Choosing workshops that fit your main path makes TAP useful for your next step.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Translating military skills into civilian words
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find civilian jobs that match your military work and describe your skills without military jargon.
This lesson builds toward: Given your military job code or title, you will find matching civilian jobs and describe your duties without military jargon, with three civilian job titles and three duties rewritten with no acronyms and at least one number.
Civilian hiring managers often do not know what your job code, rank or unit means. Your skills are real, but they need to be said in their words.
Start with free tools. O*NET's Military Crosswalk lets you search your branch's job code or title. My Next Move for Veterans, listed by the Department of Labor, has a military transition search that suggests civilian careers related to your military experience. Write down the civilian job titles they suggest.
Then translate. Replace military words with plain ones: "NCOIC" becomes "supervisor" or "team lead"; "PCS" becomes "relocation"; "mission" may become "project" or "operation". Spell out or remove acronyms. Use numbers that show size and results: how many people you led, the value of equipment you were responsible for, or how many deliveries you managed.
An AI assistant can help suggest civilian words for a duty. Describe the work in general terms only. Never paste classified, sensitive or personal information, and check that every word it suggests is true.
Step by step:
- Search your job code or title in O*NET's Military Crosswalk or My Next Move for Veterans.
- Write three civilian job titles that match.
- List your main duties in plain words.
- Replace acronyms and military terms with civilian words.
- Add numbers: people led, equipment value, tasks completed.
Words to know:
- Job code: the code for your military job, such as an MOS, rating or AFSC.
- Jargon: special words only one group understands.
- Transferable skill: a skill you can use in many different jobs, like leading a team or planning.
Official sources:
- O*NET OnLine: Military Crosswalk
- DOL VETS: Veterans employment services (My Next Move for Veterans)
Try it now: Search your military job code or title in O*NET's Military Crosswalk or My Next Move for Veterans. Write three civilian job titles it suggests, then rewrite three of your duties with no acronyms and at least one number.
You can now find civilian jobs that match your military work and describe your skills in plain civilian words.

check.q: Why translate your military skills into civilian words?
options: Civilian hiring managers may not understand military terms
Military terms are not allowed on résumés by law
To make your résumé longer
Civilian jobs do not need your skills
check.why: Hiring managers can only value skills they understand.

check.q: Your duty reads "Served as S-4 NCO for BN." What do you do?
options: Leave it as it is
Add more acronyms
Spell out or remove the acronyms and describe the work with a number
Delete the duty
check.why: Civilian bullets spell out or drop acronyms and show the size of the work.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing resume bullets for a real job
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write civilian resume bullets that match a real job posting.
This lesson builds toward: Given one real job posting, you will write civilian résumé bullets tailored to the posting, with five bullets, each with an action word, what you did and a result, and every word true.
A strong resume bullet starts with an action word, says what you did, and shows the result, ideally with a number. Pattern: action + what + result. Example: "Led a team of 12 in maintaining 30 vehicles, keeping 95% ready on schedule."
Tailor your resume to each job. Read the job posting and underline the skills and words it uses, such as "inventory", "safety", "scheduling" or "customer service". Then use those same words in your bullets, where they are true for you. Many employers use software that scans resumes for these words.
Keep it short and civilian. Usually one or two pages. Put the job title you want at the top. Leave out things that do not help this job, and do not list classified details. Add licenses and certifications, and any credentials you earned in service.
Example: a Navy logistics specialist applying for a warehouse supervisor job writes: "Managed inventory of 4,000 parts worth $2 million with 99% accuracy" and "Trained 8 new team members on safety procedures". Both use words from the posting.
Step by step:
- Find one real job posting you want.
- Underline the skills and words it uses.
- Write five bullets: action word + what you did + result with a number.
- Use the posting's words where they are true for you.
- Remove acronyms and anything classified, and read it aloud.
Words to know:
- Resume: a short document that lists your work experience, skills and education for employers.
- Tailor: to change your resume to fit one job.
- Keyword: an important word from the job posting that employers look for.
Try it now: Find one real job posting you want. Underline five skills it asks for. Write five resume bullets about your service, each with an action word, what you did and a result, using the posting's words where true.
You can now write resume bullets that turn your military experience into results a civilian employer wants.

check.q: What does it mean to tailor a résumé?
options: Use the same résumé for every job
Add every job you ever had
Make it as short as possible
Use the job posting's words where they are true for you
check.why: Tailoring matches your true experience to the words in one posting.

check.q: The posting asks for "inventory management". You tracked parts for a unit. What do you write?
options: "Did supply stuff"
"Managed inventory of 2,500 parts with no losses at audit"
"Inventory management expert with 30 years" (not true)
Leave it off
check.why: It uses the posting's words, an action word, what you did and a true result.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Networking for a civilian job
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short networking message that asks people and programs for help toward a job.
This lesson builds toward: Using people you know and veteran hiring programs, you will write a short, polite request for an informational interview and the questions you would ask, with three networking contacts or events named.
Many jobs are filled through people who know people. Networking is not begging for a job. It is making connections, asking for advice and helping others back.
Start with who you know: fellow veterans already working in civilian jobs, former leaders, family, friends, your church or community groups. Make a professional profile online, such as on LinkedIn, with a civilian headline like "Logistics supervisor, 8 years leading teams".
Ask for short informational interviews: 15 to 20 minutes to learn about someone's job and company. Prepare three questions, such as "What does a normal day look like?" and "What skills matter most here?" Thank them afterward.
Use veterans programs too. DOL's VETS lists state resources for veterans and apprenticeships, and the HIRE Vets Medallion Program recognizes employers committed to hiring veterans. Veteran job fairs and veteran groups at companies are good places to meet people.
Step by step:
- List ten people you know who work in civilian jobs.
- Make or update a professional online profile with a civilian headline.
- Ask two people for a 15-to-20-minute informational interview.
- Prepare three questions and send a thank-you afterward.
- Look up veteran job fairs and employers that hire veterans.
Words to know:
- Networking: building connections with people who can share advice, leads or introductions.
- Informational interview: a short talk to learn about someone's job, not to ask for a job.
- Headline: the short line under your name on a professional profile.
Official sources:
- DOL VETS: Veterans' Employment and Training Service
- HIRE Vets Medallion Program
Try it now: Write a list of ten people you know who work in civilian jobs. Pick two and write a short, polite message asking each for a 15-minute talk about their work. Write three questions you would ask.
You can now build a network, ask for informational interviews and use veterans hiring programs.

options: Asking strangers for a job right away
Only using social media
Building connections, asking for advice and helping others back
Sending your résumé to everyone
check.why: Networking is a two-way relationship of advice and help.

check.q: A friend works at a company you like. What do you send?
options: A short, polite request for a 15-minute talk about their work
Your résumé with "get me hired"
A two-page message about your career
Nothing; it is awkward
check.why: A short, polite request for an informational interview is easy to say yes to.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Adjusting to civilian work culture
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name key differences in civilian workplaces and plan how you will adapt.
This lesson builds toward: Given a direct order you once gave in service, you will rewrite it as a polite civilian request and list the military strengths you will keep and habits you will adjust, with two of each.
Civilian workplaces run differently. There is often no clear chain of command, and decisions may be made by groups or after long discussion. Orders may come as suggestions: "Could you take a look at this?" usually means "Please do this."
Communication is often softer. Direct, short answers that worked in uniform can sound harsh to civilian coworkers. Try adding a little context and a friendly tone. Ask questions when things are unclear; in many companies, asking is expected, not a sign of weakness.
Your strengths travel well: showing up early, finishing what you start, staying calm under pressure, and taking care of your team. Keep them. But expect less structure, less ceremony, more email and meetings, and coworkers who have never served.
It can take time to feel at home. Find a mentor at work, such as a veteran coworker, or join a veterans group if the company has one. Talk with family about the changes too: they are adjusting as well.
Step by step:
- Notice how decisions are made at your new job.
- Treat polite requests as real tasks.
- Add context and a friendly tone to direct messages.
- Ask questions when something is unclear.
- Find a mentor or a veterans group at work.
Words to know:
- Chain of command: the military order of who reports to whom.
- Workplace culture: the unwritten rules for how people work and talk at a job.
- Mentor: a more experienced person who gives you advice.
Try it now: Think of a time you gave a short, direct order in service. Rewrite it as a polite civilian request with a reason, as you would write it in a work email. Then write two military strengths you will keep and two habits you will adjust.
You can now name the main differences in civilian work culture and adjust how you communicate.

check.q: In many civilian jobs, asking questions is:
options: A sign of weakness
Expected and normal
Against the rules
Only for new hires
check.why: Civilian workplaces usually expect people to ask questions.

check.q: You want a coworker to send a report by Friday. How do you write it?
options: "Report. Friday. Now."
"Do it or else."
Say nothing and do it yourself
"Could you send the report by Friday? I need it for Monday's meeting. Thanks!"
check.why: A polite request with a reason fits civilian work culture.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Finding support and mental health care
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a support list and know how to reach crisis help any time.
This lesson builds toward: For yourself or a fellow veteran, you will create a support list that includes how to reach the Veterans Crisis Line, your nearest Vet Center and two people you trust, with the crisis numbers saved in your phone.
Leaving the military is a big change: a new routine, a new identity, maybe a move, and less contact with the people you served with. Stress, poor sleep, anger or feeling low are common. Getting help is a strength, not a weakness.
The Veterans Crisis Line is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Call 988, then press 1. Text 838255. Or chat online at veteranscrisisline.net. It is for veterans, service members, Guard and Reserve members and the people who support them, and you do not have to be enrolled in VA benefits or health care to use it.
For ongoing support, Vet Centers are community-based counseling centers that offer free, confidential counseling to eligible veterans, service members and families, including help adjusting after service. Call 1-877-927-8387 any time to talk and be connected to your nearest Vet Center. VA health care also offers mental health care for enrolled veterans.
Build your own team too: two or three people you trust, a veterans group, faith or community groups, and a regular routine with exercise and sleep. If you are worried about a fellow veteran, you can call the Crisis Line for them.
Step by step:
- Save 988 (then press 1) and the text number 838255 in your phone.
- Find your nearest Vet Center by calling 1-877-927-8387.
- Write the names and numbers of two or three people you trust.
- Add one group or routine that helps you, such as a veterans group or exercise.
- If you or a friend is in crisis, call 988 and press 1 now.
Words to know:
- Veterans Crisis Line: free, confidential, 24/7 crisis support for veterans, service members and those who support them: 988, then press 1.
- Vet Center: a community counseling center that offers free, confidential counseling to eligible veterans, service members and families.
- Confidential: kept private.
Official sources:
- Veterans Crisis Line
- VA Vet Centers
Try it now: Final task: save 988 (then press 1) and 838255 in your phone, and write your support list with your nearest Vet Center and two people you trust. Then finish your 90-day transition plan with your TAP or job services, five tailored resume bullets, three networking contacts or events, and two civilian work habits you will practice.
You can now reach crisis help any time, find ongoing support, and put your full 90-day transition plan on paper.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds TAP and job services No workshops or services named. The TAP workshops or veterans job services the learner will use, matched to their path. Includes dates or how to sign up for each. Tailored résumé bullets Fewer than five bullets, or bullets with military jargon and no results. Five bullets in civilian words, each with an action word, what was done and a result, matched to one real posting. Each bullet uses a word from the posting and has a number. Networking No people or events named. Three people or events for networking. A message is drafted for at least one, with questions to ask. Civilian work habits No habits named. Two civilian workplace habits the learner will practice. Also names two military strengths they will keep. Support list No support list, or no crisis line. The Veterans Crisis Line (988, then press 1, or text 838255), the nearest Vet Center and two trusted people. The numbers are saved in the learner's phone. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How do you reach the Veterans Crisis Line by phone?
options: Dial 988, then press 1
Dial 911, then press 9
Email your old unit
Wait for a VA appointment
check.why: The Veterans Crisis Line is 988, then press 1, any time.

check.q: You are worried about a fellow veteran who seems to be in crisis. What can you do?
options: Wait and see if it passes
Post about it online
Call the Veterans Crisis Line for them: 988, then press 1
Tell them to handle it alone
check.why: You can call the Veterans Crisis Line on behalf of someone you are worried about.
